claims.text: Standard-processed MnNiSi-based alloys exhibit a high magnetocaloric effect.
Standard-processed MnNiSi-based alloys suffer from mechanical brittleness.
Weak grain-boundary cohesion causes the mechanical brittleness of MnNiSi-based alloys.
A controlled multi-element decoration treatment during heat processing can promote preferential dopant segregation at grain boundaries.
Suitable annealing can produce a uniform grain-boundary dopant distribution without altering the bulk crystal structure.
Optimizing treatment temperature and dopant concentration can preserve the magnetocaloric phase and structural integrity.
Preferential segregation of the decorating elements enhances intergranular cohesion.
Enhanced intergranular cohesion mitigates crack initiation and propagation.
Grain-boundary accumulation of the dopants fortifies the boundaries against mechanical failure.
Localizing the dopants primarily at grain boundaries avoids significant disruption of the bulk magnetic lattice.
Avoiding significant disruption of the bulk magnetic lattice leaves the intrinsic magnetocaloric effect largely unaltered.
Multi-element grain-boundary decoration increases fracture toughness relative to an untreated MnNiSi-based control.
Multi-element grain-boundary decoration increases resistance to intergranular cracking relative to an untreated control.
The decorated material's magnetocaloric effect remains within approximately ±10% of the untreated control value.
Excessive dopant concentration can form intergranular secondary phases.
Excessive intergranular secondary phases can disrupt the uniform magnetic transition.
Excess or inappropriate dopants can produce magnetic inhomogeneity or alter the phase-transformation temperature.
